lead: Network synthesis is the reverse of circuit analysis. Analysis starts with a circuit and finds its driving-point impedance Z(s). Synthesis starts with Z(s) and asks whether a passive R, L, C one-port can produce it, and how. The answer uses two tests: the positive-real test, and the placement of poles and zeros. LC and RC one-ports have strict patterns, and Foster and Cauer forms turn those patterns into actual circuits. This matters when you must design, not just analyse, a filter or matching network.
prereq: You need the Laplace transform and network functions from Unit 5, and impedance from Unit 3.

sections.h3: Driving-point impedance and the positive-real test

blocks.text: A one-port is a network seen through one pair of terminals. Its driving-point impedance is Z(s) = V(s)/I(s), where V(s) and I(s) are the Laplace transforms of terminal voltage and current. Its driving-point admittance is Y(s) = I(s)/V(s) = 1/Z(s).

A rational function Z(s) is positive-real, written PR, when two conditions hold. First, Z(s) is real for every real value of s. Second, Re Z(s) ≥ 0 for every s with Re s > 0. For a rational function this is equivalent to: Z(s) has no poles in Re s > 0, and Re Z(jω) ≥ 0 at every frequency where Z(jω) is finite on the jω axis. A pole on the jω axis is allowed only if it is simple and its residue is non-negative. The first condition makes the coefficients real. The second says the one-port never delivers average power to a sine source.

PR is the gatekeeper test for a passive one-port. A resistor Z(s) = R passes: Re R = R ≥ 0. A capacitor Z(s) = 1/(sC) gives Re Z(jω) = 0. An inductor Z(s) = sL also gives Re Z(jω) = 0. Any network built only from R, L and C must pass the PR test.

For an LC one-port, Z(s) is a reactance function. Its finite nonzero poles and zeros are simple and lie on the jω axis. They alternate along that axis. An LC impedance may also have a pole or zero at s = 0, and may have a pole or zero at infinity; these endpoints are allowed. The finite nonzero residues are positive, and the origin and infinity terms in the Foster expansion are non-negative. The general Foster expansion is Z(s) = k∞s + k0/s + Σ 2k_i s/(s² + ω_i²), where k∞, k0 and each k_i are non-negative. The sum runs over the finite nonzero pole frequencies ω_i.

For an RC one-port, all finite nonzero poles and zeros lie on the negative real axis, at s = −σ with σ > 0. They are simple and alternate. An RC impedance may have a pole at s = 0 and a zero at infinity; these endpoints are allowed. Every finite nonzero residue is positive, and the endpoint terms have non-negative coefficients. A typical RC impedance has the form Z(s) = K∞ + K0/s + Σ K_i/(s + σ_i), with all constants non-negative.

head: One-port
Where poles and zeros lie
rows: Finite nonzero critical frequencies on jω axis; simple; alternate; positive finite residues; pole or zero at 0 or ∞ allowed
Finite nonzero critical frequencies on negative real axis; simple; alternate; positive finite residues; pole at 0 and zero at ∞ allowed

blocks.text: Positive coefficients alone do not prove realizability. A function can have all positive coefficients and still fail because its poles or zeros are in the wrong place. Check the axis and the alternation, then check the residues.

Foster forms use partial fractions. Foster I expands Z(s) into a sum of series branches. A term k0/s is a capacitor, k∞s is an inductor, and 2k_i s/(s² + ω_i²) is a parallel LC branch. Foster II expands Y(s) into a sum of parallel branches.

Cauer forms use a continued fraction. Cauer I removes a pole at infinity repeatedly, giving a ladder of series inductors and shunt capacitors. Cauer II removes a pole at zero repeatedly. The ladder is convenient when you want a physical circuit with few element values.

figure.caption: The pole and zero test depends on the axis: LC critical frequencies sit on the jω axis, RC ones on the negative real axis. Foster and Cauer are two ways to build the same function.

spec.aria: The tests differ by where poles and zeros lie; Foster and Cauer give two realization styles.

examples.question: Test whether Z(s) = (s² + 1)/(s(s² + 4)) is an LC driving-point impedance. If yes, write its Foster I form and give element values. Use s in rad/s, so element values are normalized.
steps: Write the denominator as s(s² + 4). The poles are s = 0 and s = ±j2. The numerator gives zeros at s² + 1 = 0, so s = ±j1.
The critical frequencies on the jω axis are: pole at 0, zero at 1, pole at 2. They alternate, and all are simple. This matches an LC impedance.
Expand in partial fractions: Z(s) = A/s + (Bs + C)/(s² + 4). Multiply out: A(s² + 4) + s(Bs + C) = s² + 1. Compare coefficients: 4A = 1, so A = 1/4; A + B = 1, so B = 3/4; C = 0.
The expansion is Z(s) = 1/(4s) + (3/4)s/(s² + 4). Both residues, 1/4 and 3/4, are positive, so the function is realizable.

Read the Foster I branches. The first branch 1/(4s) is a series capacitor: 1/(sC) = 1/(4s) gives C = 4 F. The second branch (3/4)s/(s² + 4) is a parallel LC branch. For parallel L and C, Z = (s/C)/(s² + 1/(LC)). Comparing, 1/C = 3/4 gives C = 4/3 F, and 1/(LC) = 4 gives L = 3/16 H.
examples.answer: Yes, it is an LC driving-point impedance. Foster I is a 4 F capacitor in series with a parallel LC branch of L = 3/16 H and C = 4/3 F, with normalized values for s in rad/s.

from fractions import Fraction
A = Fraction(1, 4)
B = Fraction(3, 4)
C1 = 1 / A
C2 = 1 / B
L = Fraction(1, 4) / C2
print(float(C1))
print(float(L))
print(float(C2))

traps: Positive coefficients do not prove an LC or RC function. Check that finite nonzero poles and zeros lie on the correct axis and alternate, with the allowed origin and infinity exceptions.
For an LC impedance, the finite nonzero residues in the partial-fraction expansion must be positive; endpoint coefficients must be non-negative. A negative residue means the function is not passive.
Do not mix up Foster I and Foster II. Foster I sums Z(s) into series branches; Foster II sums Y(s) into parallel branches.
For an RC impedance, finite nonzero critical frequencies must lie on the negative real axis. A pole at the origin and a zero at infinity are allowed; a nonzero pole on the jω axis is not.
In Foster I, the term k0/s gives C = 1/k0. Students often write C = k0 and lose the reciprocal.

quiz.q: State the two conditions for Z(s) to be positive-real.
quiz.a: Z(s) is real for every real s, and Re Z(s) ≥ 0 for every s with Re s > 0. For a rational function this also means no right-half-plane poles and Re Z(jω) ≥ 0 on the jω axis.

quiz.q: Why must the poles and zeros of an LC impedance alternate on the jω axis?
quiz.a: For a reactance function the Foster residues must be positive and the reactance slope must be positive. These conditions force simple poles and zeros to interlace on the jω axis.

quiz.q: Is Z(s) = (s² + 4)/(s(s² + 1)) an LC impedance? Give the critical frequencies and one reason.
quiz.a: No. The poles and zeros do not alternate; two poles occur before the first zero. Also the residue at ±j1 is negative, so it fails the residue test.

quiz.q: A function has all positive coefficients but a pole at s = −1 and a zero at s = −3. Can it be an RC impedance? Explain.
quiz.a: Yes, if the critical frequencies are simple, lie on the negative real axis, alternate, and all residues are positive. With only a pole at −1 and a zero at −3, check the residues; positive coefficients alone are not the proof.

quiz.q: In a Foster I LC form, a branch is 1/(4s). Find the series capacitance.
What is the difference between Foster I and Foster II?
quiz.a: Foster I expands Z(s) into series branches. Foster II expands Y(s) into parallel branches.

quiz.q: Why does Cauer I repeatedly remove a pole at infinity?
quiz.a: Removing a pole at infinity gives the next series inductor in the ladder. Repeating the removal builds the continued-fraction ladder.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, network synthesis feeds RF filter design, matching networks and integrated circuit models. CAD tools still use Foster and Cauer forms because they turn a rational function into element values. Researchers also study active and switched-capacitor synthesis, where op-amps replace inductors. Search next for Brune synthesis, Darlington synthesis, and continued-fraction ladder filters.
